meta.title: Who really said "Life Is Too Important To Be Taken Seriously"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Chesterton's maxim and not Wilde's exact words. Wilde's line is 'far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it' (Lady Windermere's Fan, 1893).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Life Is Too Important To Be Taken Seriously'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Chesterton's maxim and not Wilde's exact words. Quote Investigator traces the compressed line to Chesterton's 1902 paraphrase of Oscar Wilde.

answer.label: Not Chesterton’s maxim — his compression of Oscar Wilde
answer.sourceLine: The joke is Wilde’s, but not in these words. Lord Darlington says it in Act I of Lady Windermere’s Fan ↗ (staged 1892, published 1893) as “life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it” — the point being about talking, not about taking. Quote Investigator ↗ finds that G. K. Chesterton dropped the “talk” when he paraphrased the play in 1902, and that compressed sentence — not Wilde’s — is what now circulates under both men’s names.

source.heading: Where the sentence actually comes from

docMeta.dd: G. K. Chesterton, in print from 1902

source.excerpt:
LADY WINDERMERE: Why do you talk so trivially about life, then?
LORD DARLINGTON: Because I think that life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it.
trail: The anchor investigation is Quote Investigator ↗, which opens by stating that Wilde “did not write or say the precise quip,” walks the wording from 1893 to 1977, and concludes that a simplified version “was popularized and incorrectly attributed to Wilde by G. K. Chesterton starting in 1902” while Wilde remains “the primordial source of this family of sayings.”

We read Wilde’s own text. In Project Gutenberg’s edition of Lady Windermere’s Fan ↗, Lord Darlington’s reply in the first act reads “Because I think that life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it” — and the earlier Vera; or, The Nihilists ↗ gives Prince Paul the same joke in Act II with “much” in place of “far.” Neither play contains the compressed sentence.

The Internet Archive’s scan of Nicoll and Chesterton’s Robert Louis Stevenson ↗ (catalogued as Hodder and Stoughton, 1906) carries the sentence Quote Investigator dates to the book’s 1902 publication: “Thus the brilliant author of ‘Lady Windermere’s Fan,’ in the electric glare of modernity, finds that life is much too important to be taken seriously.” It sits in a list of paradoxes running from the Athanasian Creed through Hegel to Tertullian.

Chesterton printed it again, and marked it as a quotation. In The Ball and the Cross ↗ (1909) he writes: “Paradox of this kind is to be found in the saying of the dandy, in the decadent comedy, ‘Life is much too important to be taken seriously.’” The dandy is Lord Darlington; the decadent comedy is Wilde’s.
source.excerptNote: Wilde liked the joke enough to use it twice. In Vera; or, The Nihilists — staged in New York in 1883, its text privately printed in 1902 — Prince Paul answers a reproach in Act II with “life is much too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it.” Both versions keep the word Chesterton later dropped.

source.rightsNote: Every authored source that carries this line predates 1931 and is in the public domain in the United States: Wilde’s Lady Windermere’s Fan (Elkin Mathews and John Lane, 1893) and Vera; or, The Nihilists (privately printed, 1902), and Chesterton’s Robert Louis Stevenson (Hodder and Stoughton, 1902) and The Ball and the Cross (John Lane, 1909). The compressed popular wording has no separate authored source to protect.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: Who was Oscar Wilde?
author.bio: Born in Dublin on 16 October 1854 and dead in Paris on 30 November 1900, Wilde was an Irish author, poet and playwright whose society comedies made him the most quoted wit in London in the early 1890s. His trademark move was to hand a character a paradox and let the room fail to understand it — which is exactly what happens here, when the Duchess of Berwick begs Lord Darlington to explain himself and he declines. Because so many genuine epigrams are his, Wilde is also one of the most misquoted writers in English, and this line shows the usual mechanism: a real sentence of his, sanded down by other people until it fits on a poster.

copyAttribution: "Life is too important to be taken seriously." — a compression of Oscar Wilde, not his wording. Wilde's line, spoken by Lord Darlington in Act I of Lady Windermere's Fan (staged 1892, published 1893), is "life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it." G. K. Chesterton dropped the "talk" when paraphrasing the play in 1902. Via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Two names, one sentence, and neither wrote it that way
misattribution.intro: This line is misattributed twice over. The wording is pinned on Wilde, who never used it, and the authorship is pinned on Chesterton, who was quoting somebody else.

items.why: Quote Investigator ↗ states that Wilde “did not write or say the precise quip,” and Wikiquote ↗ files “Life is too important to be taken seriously” under Misquotations of Lord Darlington’s Act I line. Goodreads ↗ still runs the short form under Wilde’s name with no source named at all.

Chesterton is the reason the compressed sentence exists, but he never offered it as his own view. He used it in 1902 as an example of modern paradox, and in The Ball and the Cross ↗ he introduced it as “the saying of the dandy, in the decadent comedy” — a label, not a claim. QI ↗ records a Salt Lake City periodical already crediting the thought to Chesterton himself in 1910.

QI ↗ quotes a 1932 Newport, Rhode Island paper attributing “Life is too important to be taken too seriously” to an unnamed editor — one stop on a drift that ends with a 1967 syndicated television column printing the modern wording with no attribution at all.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is Wilde’s and he published it twice; the short version is Chesterton’s compression of Wilde, and the earliest instance of the exact popular wording Quote Investigator documents ↗ is a 1967 newspaper column that credits nobody.

context.heading: Chesterton wasn’t agreeing with it
lead: The irony of the Chesterton credit is that he was using the line as an exhibit, not a creed. In his 1902 essay on Robert Louis Stevenson he sets Wilde’s paradox beside the Athanasian Creed, Hegel on being and non-being, and Tertullian’s Credo quia impossibile, to argue that paradox is “inherent in all the great hypotheses of humanity” rather than a trick of light journalism.

By The Ball and the Cross ↗ in 1909 he had demoted it. There the dandy’s saying is what people see when they “look at the matter most superficially” — the shallow tier of paradox, set explicitly below “The meek shall inherit the earth.” The sentence now attributed to Chesterton is the one he offered as the lesser example.
detailsBody: Wilde’s construction does real work that the short form loses. “Too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it” is a claim about conversation: seriousness of manner is what cheapens a serious subject. “Too important to be taken seriously” is a claim about attitude, which is closer to nonsense — which is probably why it reads as a paradox worth reposting.

The drift is visible in the record Quote Investigator ↗ assembles. H. L. Mencken’s 1942 A New Dictionary of Quotations still prints Wilde’s longer form; the 1967 column prints the short one and names no one; and by the mid-1970s American newspapers were handing the short one back to Wilde as though he had written it.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator states Wilde "did not write or say the precise quip"; documents Vera (Act II, 1902 private printing) and Lady Windermere's Fan (1893) with the "talk seriously about it" wording; quotes Chesterton's 1902 Robert Louis Stevenson sentence and his 1909 Ball and the Cross instance; records the 1910 Intermountain Catholic crediting Chesterton, the 1932 Newport 'wise editor', Mencken 1942, and a 1967 unattributed instance matching the modern wording; concludes the simplified version was popularized and incorrectly attributed to Wilde by Chesterton starting in 1902, with Wilde the primordial source.

Project Gutenberg's text of Lady Windermere's Fan contains, in the FIRST ACT, LORD DARLINGTON: "Because I think that life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it.", replying to LADY WINDERMERE: "Why do you talk so trivially about life, then?"
Project Gutenberg hosts the full text of Oscar Wilde's Lady Windermere's Fan (ebook 790).

Project Gutenberg's text of Vera; or, The Nihilists contains, in ACT II, PRINCE PAUL: "Ah! my dear Count, life is much too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it.", answering COUNT R.: "There seems to be nothing in life about which you would not jest."

Project Gutenberg's text of Chesterton's The Ball and the Cross contains: "Paradox of this kind is to be found in the saying of the dandy, in the decadent comedy, 'Life is much too important to be taken seriously.'", followed by the deeper tier of paradox exemplified by "The meek shall inherit the earth."

The Internet Archive scan of Nicoll and Chesterton's Robert Louis Stevenson (item metadata: Hodder and Stoughton, 1906) contains: "Thus the brilliant author of 'Lady Windermere's Fan,' in the electric glare of modernity, finds that life is much too important to be taken seriously.", within a passage listing the Athanasian Creed, Hegel and Tertullian's "Credo quia impossibile" as paradoxes.

Wikiquote's Oscar Wilde page lists "Life is far too important a thing ever to talk seriously about it" as Lord Darlington's, Act I of Lady Windermere's Fan (1892), and lists "Life is too important to be taken seriously." beneath it under the heading "Misquotations".
Goodreads displays "Life is too important to be taken seriously." credited to Oscar Wilde, with no book or source named.
Wikipedia gives Oscar Wilde's birth date as 16 October 1854, death 30 November 1900, and describes him as "an Irish author, poet and playwright".
